Overview: Cervical spondylosis is a degenerative condition affecting the cervical spine (neck) caused by age-related wear and tear of the spinal discs, joints, and bones. It commonly occurs in middle-aged and older adults and may lead to stiffness, pain, and reduced neck mobility. In some cases, nerve compression can occur, resulting in neurological symptoms in the shoulders, arms, or hands.
Symptoms: Common symptoms of cervical spondylosis include neck pain and stiffness, headaches (especially starting from the back of the head), shoulder or arm pain, numbness or tingling in the arms or hands, muscle weakness, and reduced range of motion in the neck.
Causes: Cervical spondylosis is primarily caused by age-related degeneration of the cervical spine. Contributing factors include disc dehydration, bone spur formation, herniated discs, ligament stiffening, poor posture, repetitive neck movements, and previous neck injuries.
Preventions: Preventive measures include maintaining good posture, performing regular neck-strengthening and stretching exercises, using ergonomic workstations, avoiding prolonged screen time with poor posture, maintaining a healthy weight, and practicing proper lifting techniques.
Treatment: Treatment aims to relieve pain, improve mobility, and prevent nerve damage. Common treatments include pain relievers such as NSAIDs (Ibuprofen, Naproxen), muscle relaxants, physical therapy, posture correction exercises, and cervical traction. In severe cases where nerve compression occurs, corticosteroid injections or surgical procedures such as decompression or spinal fusion may be recommended.
When to See a Doctor: Consult a doctor if neck pain becomes severe or persistent, spreads to the arms or shoulders, or is accompanied by numbness, tingling, weakness, difficulty with coordination, or loss of bladder or bowel control. Immediate medical attention is required if symptoms worsen rapidly or significantly interfere with daily activities.
